title: Landmark Moments in Australian Law
chapters: The Communist Party case: when the High Court said no
Lindy Chamberlain and the dingo: a wrongful conviction
Mabo and the end of terra nullius

units.t: Landmark Moments in Australian Law.

In this episode: The Communist Party case: when the High Court said no, The Dismissal: Australia's 1975 constitutional crisis, Lindy Chamberlain and the dingo: a wrongful conviction and Mabo and the end of terra nullius.
Part one. The Communist Party case: when the High Court said no.
In 1950, at the height of the Cold War, the Australian Parliament banned the Communist Party.
Within months, the High Court struck the law down, in one of its most important decisions.
A Cold War law.
By 1950 the Cold War was deepening.
The Soviet Union had tested an atomic bomb, communists had won China's civil war, and the Korean War began in June, with Australian forces soon involved.
At home, a major coal strike in 1949 sharpened fears of communist influence in the unions.
Robert Menzies' Liberal and Country Party coalition won the 1949 election promising to ban the Communist Party, then a legal party.
Parliament passed the Communist Party Dissolution Act in 1950.
Labor, which controlled the Senate, was divided but let it pass.
Almost as soon as the act took effect in October, it was challenged in the High Court.
A sweeping act.
The act declared the Communist Party dissolved and its property forfeited to the Commonwealth.
On government advice, the Governor-General could also declare other organisations unlawful if they were linked to communism and judged a threat to security or defence.
Individuals could be declared too, which barred them from Commonwealth jobs and from office in certain unions.
Crucially, the act opened with recitals: statements in which Parliament itself declared that communists were working to overthrow the government by violence, and that the law was needed for defence.
People who were declared had only limited ability to challenge the government's conclusions in court.
A stream and its source.
The Communist Party and several unions argued the act exceeded federal power.
Dr H.
V.
Evatt, Labor's deputy leader and a former High Court judge, appeared for the Waterside Workers' Federation, a controversial choice.
The Commonwealth relied mainly on the defence power in section 51 of the Constitution.
The central question was whether Parliament could simply declare a threat to exist, and so give itself the power to act.
In March 1951 the High Court struck the act down by six votes to one, with Chief Justice Latham dissenting.
Whether a law falls within a head of power is for the courts to decide.
As Justice Fullagar put it, a stream cannot rise higher than its source.
Australia was not formally at war, so the defence power could not support such measures.
The rule of law assumed.
The most celebrated judgment came from Justice Owen Dixon, later Chief Justice and widely regarded as one of Australia's greatest judges.
He observed that history, and not only ancient history, shows that governments as well as private groups can undermine democratic institutions.
He added that the Constitution was framed on traditional conceptions, some of which it simply assumes, and that the rule of law is one of them.
In other words, the Constitution takes for granted that government is subject to law, enforced by independent courts.
Dixon's words are quoted in many later cases.
They help explain why Australian courts insist that judges, not ministers, set the limits of government power.
The voters decide.
The Menzies government took the question to the people.
After winning a double dissolution election in April 1951, it held a referendum in September asking voters to give the Commonwealth power over communists and communism.
Evatt, by then Labor leader, campaigned against it as a threat to civil liberties.
Early polls favoured Yes, but support fell during the campaign.
Just under half of voters said Yes, and only Queensland, Western Australia and Tasmania carried it, short of the double majority required.
The Communist Party stayed legal, never became a major electoral force, and dissolved itself in the early 1990s.
The case is still cited when courts weigh security laws, because the same question returns: who decides the limits of government?
The key idea: In 1950 the Menzies government passed a law to dissolve the Communist Party of Australia, and it was challenged almost at once.
Part two. The Dismissal: Australia's 1975 constitutional crisis.
On 11 November 1975 the Governor-General removed an elected Prime Minister from office.
Half a century later, Australians still argue about whether it was a constitutional necessity or a step too far.
11 November 1975.
Just after one o'clock on 11 November 1975, Gough Whitlam arrived at Government House in Canberra expecting a routine meeting.
Governor-General Sir John Kerr instead handed him a letter terminating his commission.
Within hours, Kerr had appointed Opposition Leader Malcolm Fraser as caretaker Prime Minister.
That afternoon, on the steps of Parliament House, Kerr's official secretary read the proclamation dissolving both houses.
Whitlam, standing behind him, told the crowd: 'Well may we say God save the Queen, because nothing will save the Governor-General.'
It is the only time a Governor-General has dismissed a federal Prime Minister.
To see why, go back several weeks to a fight over money.
A government without supply.
Governments need Parliament to approve spending through appropriation bills, called supply.
Without it, money for public servants and services eventually runs out.
Whitlam's Labor government, elected in 1972 and re-elected in 1974, controlled the House but not the Senate.
In 1975 it faced controversies, the worst being the Loans Affair, in which ministers sought a very large overseas loan through unconventional channels.
In October the Coalition, led by Fraser, used its Senate numbers to defer the supply bills until Whitlam called an election.
He refused, arguing a government's survival should depend on the House, not the Senate.
Those numbers were themselves controversial.
Two Labor Senate vacancies, in New South Wales and Queensland, were filled by non-Labor appointees, breaking the usual convention.
The states acted within their legal powers.
Kerr's decision.
Section 64 of the Constitution says ministers hold office during the Governor-General's pleasure, and section 61 gives the Governor-General executive power.
Normally these are used only on the Prime Minister's advice.
But the Governor-General also has reserve powers that can be used in rare cases without advice.
Kerr concluded that a government unable to obtain supply should either advise an election or be dismissed.
He sought the view of Chief Justice Sir Garfield Barwick, who advised in writing that dismissal was within his power.
Kerr did not warn Whitlam.
He later said he feared Whitlam would ask the Queen to remove him first.
Fraser was commissioned on condition he obtain supply and advise a double dissolution, which happened that same afternoon.
The people decide.
The dismissal unleashed fierce emotion.
Protesters gathered outside Parliament House, and Labor's slogan became a call to maintain the rage.
The House passed a no-confidence motion in Fraser, but Parliament was dissolved before the Speaker could tell the Governor-General.
At the 13 December 1975 election, the Coalition won a large majority in both houses.
Supporters called it the people's endorsement.
Critics said victory could not prove the method was proper.
Supporters argue the Senate may reject money bills, a government that cannot pay its bills cannot govern, and the voters should decide.
Critics argue the Senate should not bring down a government the House backs, Kerr should have warned Whitlam, and an unelected official should not remove an elected Prime Minister.
Some also question whether Barwick should have advised at all.
The legacy.
In 1977 voters approved a referendum requiring a replacement senator to come from the same party as the senator who left, closing the loophole exposed in 1975.
No Opposition since has blocked supply in the same way, and many observers think a new convention has formed against it.
The episode also fed later debates about whether Australia should become a republic.
In 2020, after a High Court case brought by historian Jenny Hocking, the National Archives released Kerr's correspondence with the Queen's private secretary, known as the Palace Letters.
They showed Kerr had discussed the reserve powers with the Palace beforehand, but did not tell the Queen in advance of his decision.
The key idea: On 11 November 1975 the Governor-General dismissed Prime Minister Gough Whitlam, the only time this has happened federally.
Part three. Lindy Chamberlain and the dingo: a wrongful conviction.
A baby vanished from a tent near Uluru, and her mother was convicted of murder.
It took decades, and a chance discovery, to prove the truth.
A night at Uluru.
On 17 August 1980, Michael and Lindy Chamberlain, a pastor and his wife from Mount Isa, were camping near Uluru.
Their nine-week-old daughter Azaria was asleep in the tent.
Lindy heard a cry, went to check and saw a dingo leaving.
Azaria was gone.
She was never found, though some of her clothing turned up near a dingo den a week later.
Many Australians found the story hard to believe.
Rumours spread about the family's Seventh-day Adventist faith, including the false claim that Azaria's name meant 'sacrifice in the wilderness'.
Lindy's calm in public was read as coldness.
A 1981 inquest found a dingo took the baby, but police kept investigating a murder theory.
The forensic case.
A second inquest led to Lindy being charged with murder and Michael with being an accessory after the fact.
There was no body, no confession, no clear motive and no witness to any killing.
The case rested heavily on science.
Experts testified that tests found foetal blood in the family's car, including a spray pattern under the dashboard.
A forensic expert argued that marks on the jumpsuit looked like a bloody handprint and that its damage was made by a cutting instrument, not a dingo's teeth.
The prosecution suggested Lindy had cut Azaria's throat in the car.
The Darwin jury, faced with confident experts, convicted.
In October 1982 Lindy was sentenced to life imprisonment with hard labour, and Michael received a suspended sentence.
Appeals, including to the High Court, failed.
A jacket in the sand.
Lindy had always said Azaria wore a small matinee jacket, which had never been found.
In early 1986, an English tourist, David Brett, fell to his death while climbing Uluru.
Searching for his remains, police found the jacket half buried near a dingo lair, in an area not easily reached.
It supported Lindy's account.
Within days she was released, having served more than three years.
The government set up a Royal Commission, led by Justice Trevor Morling.
His 1987 report found serious problems with the forensic evidence.
Most strikingly, the supposed spray of foetal blood under the dashboard was shown to be a sound deadening compound applied when the car was made.
Clearing their names.
Morling concluded that the convictions could not be justified on the evidence.
In September 1988 the Northern Territory Court of Criminal Appeal quashed the convictions of both Lindy and Michael.
In 1992 the Chamberlains received compensation of about 1.
3 million dollars for their wrongful imprisonment and legal costs.
Yet the official cause of death remained uncertain.
A third inquest, in 1995, returned an open finding.
Only at a fourth inquest, in June 2012, did the Northern Territory coroner, Elizabeth Morris, formally find that Azaria had been taken and killed by a dingo, and the death certificate was changed.
More than 30 years after that night, the family's account was finally recognised in law.
What the case taught.
The case is now studied as a warning about wrongful convictions.
Experts presented uncertain results with too much confidence, and some tests were poorly done or misread.
The jury had little way to know.
In the years that followed, Australian forensic science moved towards stricter standards, accreditation and more careful presentation of evidence in court.
The case also showed how media coverage and public prejudice can shape a trial, as people judged Lindy by her manner and religion rather than the facts.
Later dingo attacks on children, including a fatal attack on Fraser Island, now K'gari, in 2001, ended any lingering doubt that dingoes can be dangerous.
Above all, a conviction is only as strong as its evidence.
The key idea: Azaria Chamberlain vanished from a tent in 1980, and public suspicion turned on her parents.
Part four. Mabo and the end of terra nullius.
In 1992 a man from a tiny island in the Torres Strait changed the foundations of Australian land law.
The Mabo decision overturned a legal fiction that had stood since 1788 and reshaped the national conversation about who owns the country.
A garden on Mer.
Mer, or Murray Island, is a small volcanic island in the eastern Torres Strait.
For generations the Meriam people have tended gardens there, with plots passed down through families under their own laws.
Eddie Koiki Mabo grew up on Mer and later worked on the mainland, including as a gardener at James Cook University in Townsville.
In the 1970s academics there told him that under Australian law his family's land belonged to the Crown.
To Mabo this made no sense.
The law rested on a fiction often called terra nullius, Latin for land belonging to no one: that the continent in 1788 had no recognisable system of ownership.
A 1971 case, Milirrpum v Nabalco, brought by Yolngu people, accepted they had a sophisticated system of law but ruled it gave no property rights recognised by Australian law.
A ten-year fight.
In 1982 Eddie Mabo and four other Meriam people, including David Passi and James Rice, began a High Court case claiming their traditional land rights on Mer.
In 1985 the Queensland Government passed a law declaring any such rights had been wiped out when the islands were annexed in 1879.
In 1988, in Mabo No 1, the High Court struck that law down because it was inconsistent with the federal Racial Discrimination Act.
The main case then returned to fact-finding, with weeks of evidence about Meriam customs and land holding.
It was gruelling, expensive and slow.
Eddie Mabo died of cancer in January 1992, months before the final decision.
The decision.
On 3 June 1992, in Mabo v Queensland No 2, the High Court ruled six judges to one that the Meriam people held native title to most of the land on Mer.
More broadly, it held that Australia's common law recognises native title, reflecting the rights of Indigenous peoples under their traditional laws and customs.
The judges rejected the idea that the land belonged to no one as a basis for denying those rights, calling it out of step with history and modern values.
But the decision set limits.
Valid government acts, such as granting freehold, can extinguish native title, and it survives only where a group has kept up its connection with the land.
From ruling to law.
The decision raised urgent questions.
After negotiating with Indigenous leaders, industry and the states, the Keating government passed the Native Title Act 1993.
It confirmed existing titles, set up a claims process and created the National Native Title Tribunal; the Federal Court decides or approves claims.
After the 1996 Wik decision found pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title, the Howard government passed major amendments in 1998.
Native title does not threaten suburban backyards, because freehold generally extinguishes it.
What it includes depends on a group's traditional laws and the rights already over the land.
Sometimes it means exclusive possession.
More often it is shared rights to camp, hunt, fish, hold ceremonies or be consulted, alongside pastoralists, miners or the public.
Proving a claim can be very hard for peoples forcibly moved off their country.
A lasting legacy.
Reactions were sharply divided in the 1990s.
Some business groups and politicians warned of uncertainty for mining and farming, while many Indigenous advocates felt the system that followed gave them too little.
Over time, native title has been recognised over a large share of the continent, often through negotiated agreements rather than courtroom battles, though the rights involved vary greatly.
The anniversary of the judgment, 3 June, is now marked as Mabo Day.
It closes National Reconciliation Week, which begins on 27 May, the date of the 1967 referendum.
Eddie Mabo did not live to see his victory, but his name marks the moment Australian law formally recognised that the land had owners long before 1788.
The key idea: Eddie Mabo discovered that Australian law gave his family's island land to the Crown, on the fiction that the continent had no owners.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was the main aim of the Communist Party Dissolution Act of 1950?
Answer. To dissolve the Communist Party of Australia.
Question two. What made 11 November 1975 unusual?
Answer. A Governor-General dismissed an elected Prime Minister.
Question three. What fed public suspicion of the Chamberlains?
Answer. Rumours about their faith and Lindy's calm manner.
Question four. What did Mabo's case challenge?
Answer. The idea that the continent had no owners in 1788.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
